_meta.about: Curated, human-verified resources per topic code. Keyed by code (e.g. MIND.01). Loaded at runtime by index.html and merged over the search fallback; any code without an entry keeps its Watch/Read search links. See CURATING.md for the schema and quality rubric, and run `npm run verify-links` after every change.
_meta.knownVerifierWarnings: britannica.com, newsinhealth.nih.gov, and aeon.co bot-wall or rate-limit automated checkers, so verify-links.js reports them as WARN. All three were confirmed to return HTTP 200 in a real browser on 2026-07-16 — WARN here means 'checker was blocked', not 'link is dead'.

MIND.01.note: Article explains the effect and cites the source study; deeper is the original Norton/Mochon/Ariely paper. No video cleared the bar, so Watch stays on search.

deeper.title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love (Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 2012)
deeper.source: Norton, Mochon and Ariely — Harvard Business School

exercise.prompt: Compare how much you value two similar objects or outputs when you assembled one yourself, then identify effort, ownership and quality as competing explanations.

MIND.02.note: Jarrett is the definitive 'the pop story is overhyped' piece; deeper is the Kilner and Lemon review that the critique rests on. Video stays on search to avoid overclaiming.

article.title: Mirror Neurons: The Most Hyped Concept in Neuroscience?

deeper.title: What We Know Currently about Mirror Neurons
deeper.source: Kilner and Lemon — Current Biology / PubMed Central

exercise.prompt: Separate what mirror-neuron experiments directly measure from claims about imitation, empathy, language and autism, then label each claim as evidence, inference or speculation.

MIND.03.note: Schwartz's TED talk is the claim; Collins and the Scheibehenne meta-analysis provide the replication reality. Pairing them is the honest version of this topic.

deeper.title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
deeper.source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd — Journal of Consumer Research

exercise.prompt: Design a choice experiment that varies number of options while holding quality, familiarity and decision stakes constant, then define what would count as overload.

MIND.04.note: The hook frames synchronicity as contested and pattern hunger. The curated resource therefore explains patternicity rather than endorsing a supernatural interpretation.

article.title: Patternicity: Finding Meaningful Patterns in Meaningless Noise

exercise.prompt: Keep a one-week log of striking coincidences and also record the ordinary non-matches that could have become coincidences, then compare remembered hits with the full opportunity set.

MIND.05.note: Neuroplasticity is heavily hyped; Britannica supplies a sober overview that avoids the self-help claim that any habit can freely rewire any brain function.

exercise.prompt: Classify examples of plasticity as developmental, learning-related, compensatory or injury-related and identify biological constraints on each.

MIND.06.note: Britannica provides the concept; the deeper resource is Festinger and Carlsmith's founding forced-compliance experiment.

deeper.title: Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance
deeper.source: Festinger and Carlsmith — Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology / MIT

exercise.prompt: Map one inconsistency among belief, action and self-image, then list several possible dissonance-reduction strategies and the evidence each would leave behind.

MIND.07.note: The catalogue emphasizes the statistical critique, so the resource explains how random data, measurement boundaries and regression effects can reproduce the familiar graph.

article.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect Is Probably Not Real
article.source: Jonathan Jarry — McGill Office for Science and Society

exercise.prompt: Generate random true scores and noisy self-assessments, group people by observed performance and graph average error to see how statistical artefacts can resemble the published effect.

MIND.08.note: Csikszentmihalyi's own TED talk supplies the primary popular account; BrainFacts provides a neuroscience-oriented secondary view without turning flow into a productivity guarantee.

article.title: Turning on Flow Means Turning Off Parts of the Brain

exercise.prompt: Choose one activity and vary challenge, skill, goals and feedback over several sessions, recording boredom, anxiety, absorption and performance rather than assuming flow occurred.

MIND.09.note: TED-Ed provides the accessible mechanism, NIH gives the overview, and the Rasch and Born review is the deeper open-access source on sleep-dependent memory consolidation.

video.title: The Benefits of a Good Night's Sleep

article.title: Sleep On It: How Snoozing Strengthens Memories

deeper.title: About Sleep's Role in Memory
deeper.source: Rasch and Born — Physiological Reviews / PubMed Central

exercise.prompt: Learn two matched sets of material before sleep and before an equally long waking interval, test delayed recall and identify the controls needed before attributing differences to consolidation.

MIND.10.note: Anil Seth supplies the accessible on-ramp to predictive perception; Andy Clark's review is the field-defining deeper treatment of prediction, action and error correction.

video.title: Your Brain Hallucinates Your Conscious Reality

article.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness Is a Distraction from the Real One

deeper.title: Whatever Next? Predictive Brains, Situated Agents, and the Future of Cognitive Science
deeper.source: Andy Clark — Behavioral and Brain Sciences / UCL

exercise.prompt: Use one ambiguous image or sound to describe prior expectation, sensory evidence, prediction error and how changing context alters the final percept.

MIND.11.note: Nielsen's essay is the strongest single practical treatment of spaced repetition as a system for building long-term understanding rather than merely memorizing isolated trivia.

exercise.prompt: Create ten atomic retrieval cards from one difficult concept, schedule them over two weeks and revise cards that produce guessing, ambiguity or rote wording without understanding.

MIND.12.note: The resource debunks the fabricated '38 silent witnesses' version of Kitty Genovese and summarizes modern evidence showing that help is common and can increase with more bystanders.

article.title: The Bystander Effect Started from a Lie
article.source: Jonathan Jarry — McGill Office for Science and Society

exercise.prompt: Break an emergency response into noticing, interpreting, taking responsibility, knowing what to do and acting, then design instructions that reduce ambiguity at each stage.

PRAX.01.note: Stanford's Zen entry discusses mushin as no-mind within a larger philosophical and embodied practice, avoiding the pop-performance caricature.

exercise.prompt: Choose one well-learned physical skill and describe which parts can become automatic, which still require attention, and why mushin is not mere mindlessness.

PRAX.02.note: The paired Stanford entries distinguish the wider existentialist tradition from Camus's self-described philosophy of the absurd and his criticism of existentialist escape routes.

exercise.prompt: Compare Sartrean meaning-making and Camusian revolt in a two-column table, then apply both responses to the same meaningless setback.

PRAX.03.note: Taleb and Douady's paper gives antifragility a mathematical definition through convex response to variability rather than treating it as a vague synonym for resilience.

article.title: Mathematical Definition, Mapping, and Detection of (Anti)Fragility
article.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb and Raphaël Douady — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Draw one concave and one convex response curve and explain why added variability harms the first system but can benefit the second.

PRAX.04.note: Cornell's official guide provides a concrete, evidence-oriented note workflow with capture, cue, summary, recitation, reflection, and review.

exercise.prompt: Take one page of Cornell notes from a lecture or article, add retrieval questions in the cue column, and write a five-sentence summary without looking back.

PRAX.05.note: Stanford presents Stoic logic, physics, and ethics as one system, correcting the modern reduction of Stoicism to emotional suppression.

exercise.prompt: For one current problem, separate what is up to you from what is not, then write one action guided by virtue rather than by outcome control.

PRAX.06.note: The original passage in Chesterton's The Thing is used instead of later paraphrases, preserving his argument about understanding an institution before reforming it.

article.title: The Thing — The Drift from Domesticity

exercise.prompt: Choose one annoying rule or legacy feature, investigate the failure it originally prevented, and propose a replacement that preserves that function.

PRAX.07.note: Stanford's current identity-over-time entry uses Theseus' ship to introduce competing accounts of persistence, constitution, replacement, and reassembly.

exercise.prompt: Apply the Ship of Theseus puzzle to a software system whose modules are gradually rewritten, then define three different criteria for calling it the same system.

PRAX.08.note: Stanford's simplicity entry separates evidential, pragmatic, syntactic, and ontological simplicity and explains why Occam's Razor is not simply 'pick the easiest story.'

exercise.prompt: Compare two explanations by counting assumptions, parameters, predictive consequences, and ad hoc exceptions rather than judging which sounds simpler.

PRAX.09.note: Yale's lecture introduces the classic trolley cases within a broader course on moral psychology, consequentialism, intention, and doing versus allowing harm.

exercise.prompt: Compare switch, footbridge, and loop variants, stating what changes in intention, physical means, personal force, and expected consequences.

PRAX.10.note: Stanford's Daoism entry situates wu wei within early Chinese debates about action, guidance, spontaneity, and non-coercive rule.

exercise.prompt: Identify one task where extra force creates resistance, then redesign the process around timing, environment, and response rather than direct control.

PRAX.11.note: Ericsson and Harwell clarify the original definition of deliberate practice and distinguish structured improvement from accumulated hours or casual repetition.

article.title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance
article.source: K. Anders Ericsson and Kyle W. Harwell — Frontiers in Psychology

exercise.prompt: Turn one broad skill into a 30-minute practice block with a narrow target, measurable error, immediate feedback, repetition, and reflection.

PRAX.12.note: The resource covers the classical via negativa—speaking by negation about what exceeds concepts—while the exercise carefully adapts subtraction as a practical heuristic.

exercise.prompt: Take one overloaded routine or system and remove one element at a time, recording which removals preserve the goal and which destroy a necessary function.

MATH.01.note: Stanford's entry explains the first and second incompleteness theorems, their formal assumptions, and common overstatements about what Gödel proved.

exercise.prompt: Write down the difference between consistency, completeness, and decidability, then explain which property each incompleteness theorem limits.

MATH.02.note: The Stanford entry develops Bayes' theorem from conditional probability and distinguishes the mathematical rule from broader Bayesian inference.

exercise.prompt: Choose a medical-test example with a low base rate and calculate the posterior probability after one positive result.

MATH.03.note: Stanford's set-theory overview introduces cardinality, Cantor's theory of the infinite, and why different infinite sets can have different sizes.

exercise.prompt: Construct a diagonal argument showing that binary sequences cannot be completely listed, then connect it to the uncountability of the real numbers.

MATH.04.note: The Clay Mathematics Institute gives the official Millennium Prize framing of efficient verification, efficient solution, and the significance of P versus NP.

exercise.prompt: Take one search problem such as Sudoku or travelling salesperson and separate the work needed to verify a proposed answer from the work needed to find one.

MATH.05.note: MIT's signals-and-systems lecture treats the Fourier transform as the continuous-frequency extension of Fourier-series analysis.

exercise.prompt: Generate a signal made from two sine waves, plot it in time, compute its discrete Fourier transform, and identify the two frequency peaks.

MATH.06.note: MathWorld gives a compact derivation and reference treatment of Euler's formula, from which Euler's identity follows by substituting pi.

exercise.prompt: Use the power-series expansions of exponential, sine, and cosine to derive Euler's formula term by term.

MATH.07.note: Scholarpedia's expert-authored history connects nonlinear dynamical systems, sensitive dependence, attractors, bifurcations, and deterministic chaos.

exercise.prompt: Iterate the logistic map for two initial values that differ only in the sixth decimal place and graph how their trajectories separate.

MATH.08.note: MIT's plane-geometry and topology course supplies an accessible route into continuity, deformation, winding, and topological invariants.

article.title: Geometry and Topology in the Plane

exercise.prompt: Classify several drawn shapes by connected components and holes, then explain which can be continuously deformed into one another.

MATH.09.note: NIST's Monte Carlo tool and documentation provide a practical institutional introduction to simulation-based uncertainty analysis.

article.title: Monte Carlo Tool
article.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

exercise.prompt: Estimate pi by sampling random points in a square, counting those inside the inscribed circle, and plotting error against sample size.

MATH.10.note: NIST's normal-distribution handbook entry explains the distribution and explicitly identifies the central limit theorem as its main theoretical justification.

exercise.prompt: Simulate repeated samples from a strongly skewed distribution and compare histograms of the raw values with histograms of their sample means.

MATH.11.note: MIT's opening graph-theory lecture introduces graphs as mathematical objects and connects structural questions to modern combinatorics.

article.title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics

exercise.prompt: Model the Seven Bridges of Königsberg as a graph, calculate every vertex degree, and use Euler's criterion to explain why the walk is impossible.

MATH.12.note: Princeton's programming assignment turns the birthday collision result into an experiment and connects probability calculations with simulation.

exercise.prompt: Simulate rooms of increasing size until the shared-birthday probability crosses 50 percent, then compare the simulation with the exact formula.

COSM.01.note: Stanford's philosophy-of-time entry maps the main disputes about passage, persistence, past and future reality, and time's relation to physics.

exercise.prompt: Compare presentism, eternalism, and the growing-block view in a table, including what each says exists now.

COSM.02.note: The Stanford entry separates thermodynamic irreversibility, statistical mechanics, boundary conditions, and the arrow of time instead of reducing entropy to vague disorder.

exercise.prompt: Describe one reversible microscopic process and one irreversible macroscopic process, then identify the statistical assumption connecting them.

COSM.03.note: The SETI Institute presents the paradox, its assumptions, the Drake-equation context, and major families of proposed resolutions.

exercise.prompt: List five possible filters or explanations for the silence, then rank them by how much evidence would be needed to distinguish them.

COSM.04.note: Einstein Online's Elementary Einstein collection provides connected introductions to special relativity, spacetime, gravity, and general relativity.

article.title: Elementary Einstein
article.source: Einstein Online — Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics

exercise.prompt: Calculate the Lorentz factor at several fractions of light speed and explain why Newtonian time is a good approximation at everyday speeds.

COSM.05.note: The Nobel Prize's 2022 popular information explains entanglement, Bell inequalities, and the experiments that ruled out broad classes of local hidden-variable models.

article.title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 — Popular Information

exercise.prompt: Write a plain-language explanation of correlation, entanglement, and Bell inequality violation without using faster-than-light messaging as an explanation.

COSM.06.note: OpenStax develops double-slit interference quantitatively and shows how path difference produces bright and dark fringes.

exercise.prompt: Use the double-slit fringe-spacing formula to predict how the pattern changes when wavelength, slit spacing, or screen distance is doubled.

COSM.07.note: NASA's universe overview distinguishes ordinary matter, dark matter, and dark energy and summarizes the observations used to infer each component.

exercise.prompt: Create an evidence table for dark matter and dark energy, separating what is directly observed from what is inferred.

COSM.08.note: CERN's official overview explains the Standard Model's matter particles, force carriers, Higgs field, successes, and known omissions.

exercise.prompt: Recreate the Standard Model table from memory, grouping quarks, leptons, and bosons and adding charge and force interaction notes.

COSM.09.note: David Wallace's review explains precisely why combining black-hole evaporation with ordinary quantum mechanics appears to destroy information.

article.title: Why Black Hole Information Loss is Paradoxical

exercise.prompt: Write the paradox as a sequence of assumptions and identify which assumption each major proposed resolution must reject or modify.

COSM.10.note: NASA's WMAP overview explains the microwave background as relic radiation and connects its measured fluctuations to the age, geometry, and composition of the universe.

exercise.prompt: Explain why the cosmic microwave background is not light from the Big Bang instant itself and what the anisotropy map measures.

COSM.11.note: NASA's discussion of dark energy and cosmic expansion provides the observational basis for considering long-term expansion-dominated futures, including increasingly cold and dilute outcomes.

exercise.prompt: Compare heat death, Big Crunch, and Big Rip scenarios by stating the required expansion behavior and the final availability of usable energy.

COSM.12.note: The Santa Fe Institute introduces complex-systems science through nonlinearity, collective dynamics, hierarchy, randomness, and emergence.

exercise.prompt: Choose an emergent system and identify its agents, local rules, feedback loops, macro-pattern, and why the macro-pattern is not written into any one rule.

VITA.01.note: NHGRI explains epigenomic marks, gene regulation, development, environmental response, and the limited senses in which marks can persist through cell division or generations.

exercise.prompt: Draw how DNA methylation and histone modification can alter gene expression without changing nucleotide sequence, then distinguish mitotic from transgenerational inheritance.

VITA.02.note: NHGRI's genome-editing overview explains targeted cutting and repair, why CRISPR changed the field, and the difference between research use and clinical application.

exercise.prompt: Sketch a CRISPR-Cas9 edit from guide-RNA targeting through DNA cutting and repair, comparing knockout by end joining with precise editing by a repair template.

VITA.03.note: This review balances established roles in metabolism and immunity with unresolved definitions of a healthy microbiome and uncertainty about whether many associations are causes or consequences.

article.title: Establishing What Constitutes a Healthy Human Gut Microbiome: State of the Science, Regulatory Considerations, and Future Directions
article.source: National Academies workshop authors — PubMed Central

exercise.prompt: Take one microbiome-health headline and classify its evidence as association, mechanism, animal experiment, or human causal trial, noting plausible confounders.

VITA.04.note: OpenStax presents the evidence that mitochondria and plastids descend from engulfed bacteria, including membranes, DNA, ribosomes, and gene transfer.

exercise.prompt: Create an evidence table for endosymbiosis covering double membranes, circular DNA, ribosomes, binary fission, phylogeny, and transferred nuclear genes.

VITA.05.note: DeepMind's official AlphaFold overview explains sequence-to-structure prediction and its scientific impact while leaving experimental validation and protein dynamics visible as separate problems.

exercise.prompt: Look up one protein in AlphaFold DB and identify high- and low-confidence regions, then list questions a static prediction cannot answer about function or dynamics.

VITA.06.note: CDC explains antigens, adaptive immune memory, vaccine platforms, and why temporary immune symptoms differ from the disease being prevented.

article.title: Explaining How Vaccines Work
article.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

exercise.prompt: Trace antigen presentation, helper T-cell signalling, B-cell activation, antibodies, and memory cells after vaccination, then compare first and later exposure.

VITA.07.note: OpenStax distinguishes convergent from divergent evolution and shows how similar selection pressures can independently produce analogous traits.

exercise.prompt: Compare wings in bats, birds, and insects, distinguishing shared function, developmental origin, homology, analogy, and the selection pressure involved.

VITA.08.note: OpenStax connects chloroplast structure, pigments, light reactions, carbon fixation, and energy storage in a standard biology treatment.

exercise.prompt: Draw the light reactions and Calvin cycle, labelling where photons, water, oxygen, ATP, NADPH, carbon dioxide, and carbohydrate enter or leave.

VITA.09.note: WHO's current fact sheet explains natural selection for resistance, misuse and overuse, transmission across humans, animals and environments, and the public-health consequences.

exercise.prompt: Model a bacterial population before and after antibiotic exposure and explain selection, mutation, horizontal transfer, incomplete treatment, and transmission without saying bacteria choose to adapt.

VITA.10.note: NIGMS explains molecular clocks, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peripheral clocks, environmental cues, and the consequences of chronic misalignment.

article.title: Circadian Rhythms
article.source: National Institute of General Medical Sciences

exercise.prompt: Track light exposure, meals, exercise, sleepiness, and sleep timing for three days, then identify cues that may advance, delay, or desynchronise your clocks.

VITA.11.note: NIA explains telomeres as chromosome-end protection and places shortening among several interacting ageing processes rather than presenting it as a single master clock.

exercise.prompt: Draw the trade-off between unlimited cell division and tumour suppression, including telomere shortening, telomerase, senescence, apoptosis, stem cells, and cancer.

VITA.12.note: OpenStax gives a quantitative account of resting potential, threshold, voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, refractory periods, and propagation.

exercise.prompt: Plot membrane voltage over time and label rest, threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, sodium-channel state, potassium-channel state, and refractory periods.

ENGN.01.note: IMAX's official overview explains the integrated system of large-format capture, projection, sound, screen geometry, and theatre design rather than treating IMAX as only a screen size.

exercise.prompt: Compare standard cinema and IMAX by capture format, image area, projection, aspect ratio, screen geometry, seating field of view, and sound system.

ENGN.02.note: Formula 1's technical explainer uses a current race car to connect wing profiles, pressure differences, ground effect, downforce, drag, and setup compromises.

article.title: F1 EXPLAINS: Downforce and why F1 cars have wings — with McLaren aero specialist Emel Cankaya

exercise.prompt: Draw the aerodynamic forces on an F1 car and explain how increasing wing angle changes cornering grip, tyre load, drag, top speed, and energy use.

ENGN.03.note: The Bluetooth SIG overview introduces the radio, protocol stack, topology, Classic and Low Energy modes, frequency use, and interoperability ecosystem.

exercise.prompt: Trace a Bluetooth Low Energy connection from advertising and scanning through connection, service discovery, characteristic access, and disconnection.

ENGN.04.note: Intel's manufacturing overview follows processor fabrication from purified silicon and wafers through repeated deposition, lithography, etching, doping, interconnect, testing, cutting, and packaging.

exercise.prompt: Create a process flow from silicon ingot to packaged CPU and mark which stages add material, remove material, change electrical properties, or inspect defects.

ENGN.05.note: D23's animation glossary entry explains the transparent celluloid layer that allowed moving characters to be painted separately from reusable backgrounds.

article.title: Cel
article.source: D23 — The Official Disney Fan Club

exercise.prompt: Plan a two-second animation on twos: draw 12 numbered poses, identify keyframes and in-betweens, and separate the moving subject from a reusable background.

ENGN.06.note: NASA's propulsion guide explains the compressor, combustor, turbine and nozzle, then distinguishes turbojet, turbofan, turboprop and turboshaft arrangements.

exercise.prompt: Label a turbofan cutaway and track pressure, temperature, velocity, energy transfer, and airflow through fan, compressor, combustor, turbine, bypass and nozzle.

ENGN.07.note: BYU's acoustics group explains active noise control as destructive interference produced through sensing, processing, and secondary sound sources, including practical limitations.

article.title: Active Noise Control
article.source: Brigham Young University Acoustics Research Group

exercise.prompt: Draw a feedforward ANC system with reference microphone, adaptive filter, speaker, error microphone and listener, then explain why low steady frequencies are easiest to cancel.

ENGN.08.note: WSDOT's Tacoma Narrows history explains the load path of suspension bridges and uses the 1940 failure to show why aerodynamic stability must be designed, not assumed.

deeper.title: Why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge Collapsed

exercise.prompt: Draw the load path from deck to suspenders, main cables, towers and anchorages, then add wind-induced torsion and the design features used to resist it.

ENGN.09.note: The NRC definition identifies the universal reactor functions: controlled fission, fuel, moderation where applicable, neutron economy, cooling, monitoring, control rods, shielding and protection.

exercise.prompt: Draw a thermal reactor and explain the separate jobs of fuel, moderator, coolant, control rods, pressure boundary, steam system, containment and emergency cooling.

ENGN.10.note: DOE explains batteries through chemical potential, electron flow in the external circuit, ion flow through electrolyte, charging reversibility, degradation and safety research.

article.title: DOE Explains...Batteries
article.source: U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science

exercise.prompt: Draw charge and discharge for a lithium-ion cell, showing electron and ion directions, anode, cathode, electrolyte, separator and one pathway to thermal runaway.

ENGN.11.note: GPS.gov explains the space, control and user segments, satellite time broadcasts and receiver positioning; its trilateration activity turns signal travel time into measured distance.

exercise.prompt: Use four simulated satellite positions and travel times to solve receiver location and clock offset, then list atmospheric, orbital and multipath error sources.

ENGN.12.note: OpenStax connects focal length, aperture, shutter and image formation to the sensor plane, giving the optical foundation beneath digital-camera electronics.

exercise.prompt: Photograph one subject using different focal lengths, apertures and shutter speeds, then explain changes in angle of view, perspective, depth of field, motion and sensor exposure.

INFR.01.note: TeleGeography's continuously maintained FAQ explains fibre construction, routing, ownership, capacity, landing, repair, faults and why satellites carry only a small share of international traffic.

exercise.prompt: Use the submarine cable map to trace two independent routes between South Africa and Europe, then identify shared landing or geographic failure points.

INFR.02.note: DOE explains generation, transmission, substations and distribution, then shows why system operators must continuously balance real power to protect frequency and reliability.

deeper.title: Keeping the Lights On: Essential Reliability Services

exercise.prompt: Simulate a generator trip on a supply-demand graph and sequence inertia, primary frequency response, automatic control, dispatch and load shedding.

INFR.03.note: The Smithsonian account connects Malcolm McLean's experiment, intermodal transfer, port transformation, labour disruption and standard boxes as one system innovation.

article.title: Transforming the Waterfront
article.source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

exercise.prompt: Map one container from factory to customer, including stuffing, trucking, terminal gate, crane, vessel, customs, rail or road transfer, empty return and documentation.

INFR.04.note: CDC explains the conventional drinking-water train; EPA's municipal wastewater primer adds preliminary, primary, biological secondary and advanced treatment before discharge or reuse.

article.title: How Water Treatment Works
article.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

deeper.title: Primer for Municipal Wastewater Treatment Systems

exercise.prompt: Draw the complete urban water loop from source through drinking treatment, distribution, household use, sewer collection, wastewater treatment, receiving water and possible reuse.

INFR.05.note: ICAO frames air traffic management as a total system combining airspace organization, communication, navigation, surveillance, separation assurance, collision avoidance and traffic-flow optimization.

exercise.prompt: Plan two crossing flights through controlled airspace and show how clearances, altitude, route, surveillance, handoffs, flow control and separation minima prevent conflict.

INFR.06.note: Nobel's account links Haber's catalytic ammonia synthesis to Bosch's engineering of a safe, durable high-pressure industrial process and large-scale fertilizer production.

exercise.prompt: Apply Le Châtelier's principle to nitrogen plus hydrogen forming ammonia and explain the engineering trade-offs among pressure, temperature, catalyst, conversion, recycle and energy use.

INFR.07.note: The American Cement Association separates cement from concrete and explains hydration, aggregate binding, placement, curing, strength development and durability.

exercise.prompt: Compare four mixes by water-cement ratio, aggregate, curing and reinforcement, predicting workability, porosity, compressive strength, cracking and embodied emissions.

INFR.08.note: WHO treats the cold chain as an end-to-end quality system involving forecasting, packaging, storage, transport, monitoring, stock control, equipment and contingency planning.

exercise.prompt: Design a cold-chain route to a remote clinic, including temperature range, packaging, data loggers, storage capacity, transport delays, power failure and product quarantine rules.

INFR.09.note: The U.S. Treasury's acquiring-service explanation clearly separates the real-time authorization message from later clearing, net obligations and interbank settlement.

article.title: How CAS Works
article.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury — Bureau of the Fiscal Service

exercise.prompt: Trace a card purchase through cardholder, merchant, gateway or processor, acquirer, network and issuer during authorization, capture, clearing, settlement and chargeback.

INFR.10.note: ISO explains standards as expert consensus that creates repeatable specifications, interoperability, safety, quality and access to markets rather than rules chosen by a single vendor.

exercise.prompt: Choose one everyday interface and list the dimensions, protocols, tests, terminology and governance that must be standardized for products from different firms to interoperate.

INFR.11.note: NIST describes the semiconductor supply chain as globally distributed, highly specialized and dependent on thousands of suppliers, with important geographic concentrations in tools and materials.

article.title: Vision for Success: Facilities for Semiconductor Materials and Manufacturing Equipment
article.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

exercise.prompt: Map the supply chain for one advanced chip across design software, architecture IP, wafers, chemicals, lithography, fabrication, packaging, testing and final assembly, marking single points of concentration.

INFR.12.note: The NTP Project explains the hierarchy of reference clocks and servers, timestamp exchange, network-delay estimation, clock discipline, UTC and leap-second complications.

exercise.prompt: Record four NTP timestamps, calculate round-trip delay and clock offset, then explain asymmetry, drift, stratum, leap seconds and why monotonic time differs from wall-clock time.

COMP.01.note: Cloudflare provides a concise end-to-end overview of packets, protocols, routing, TCP, TLS, DNS, and HTTP without hiding the distributed nature of the Internet.

exercise.prompt: Open the browser Network panel, reload a website, and identify the DNS lookup, connection, request, response, and transferred resources.

COMP.02.note: This resource covers recursive resolvers, authoritative nameservers, the lookup hierarchy, caching, and the distinction between domain names and IP addresses.

article.title: What is DNS? | How DNS works

exercise.prompt: Run dig or nslookup against one domain. Record its A or AAAA record, TTL, authoritative nameserver, and any CNAME chain.

COMP.03.note: Cloudflare explains BGP through autonomous systems, route advertisements, path selection, trust assumptions, and common security weaknesses.

article.title: What is BGP? | BGP routing explained

exercise.prompt: Draw five autonomous systems with two possible routes between a client and server. Mark which route BGP would advertise and how a false shorter route could hijack traffic.

COMP.04.note: The article clearly separates public-key encryption, private keys, authentication, key exchange, and the symmetric session keys later used by TLS.

article.title: How does public key cryptography work?

exercise.prompt: Write a four-step message exchange showing which key Alice and Bob use for encryption, decryption, signing, and signature verification.

COMP.05.note: Crafting Interpreters teaches scanning, parsing, syntax trees, evaluation, bytecode, virtual machines, and garbage collection by implementing two complete interpreters.

exercise.prompt: Implement a tokenizer for numbers, identifiers, parentheses, and the four arithmetic operators. Print the resulting token stream.

COMP.06.note: The OSTEP scheduling chapter develops FIFO, SJF, STCF, round-robin, response time, turnaround time, preemption, context-switch cost, and I/O overlap.

article.title: Scheduling: Introduction
article.source: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces — Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau

exercise.prompt: Given three jobs with different arrival and execution times, calculate average turnaround and response time under FIFO, SJF, STCF, and round-robin.

COMP.07.note: PostgreSQL documentation precisely defines dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantom reads, serialization anomalies, and the guarantees of each implemented isolation level.

exercise.prompt: Open two database sessions and reproduce a nonrepeatable read or serialization failure. Repeat the test under a stronger isolation level.

COMP.08.note: The Raft project provides the accessible model and visualization; the original USENIX paper provides the formal algorithm, safety argument, elections, and replicated-log design.

deeper.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm
deeper.source: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout — USENIX ATC 2014

exercise.prompt: Simulate a five-node Raft cluster. Trigger a leader failure, elect a replacement, and explain why a majority is required to commit a log entry.

COMP.09.note: Sipser introduces diagonalization and reducibility before showing that the Turing-machine halting problem is undecidable.

exercise.prompt: Write the assumed HALTS(program, input) function, then construct the self-referential program that produces a contradiction when called with itself.

COMP.10.note: Jay Alammar supplies the visual intuition for embeddings, query-key-value projections, self-attention, multiple heads, positional encoding, and decoding. The NeurIPS paper is the primary source.

exercise.prompt: Using three small vectors, calculate one scaled dot-product attention output by hand: QKᵀ, scaling, softmax, and multiplication by V.

COMP.11.note: Princeton connects prefix-free codes, Huffman coding, LZW, entropy, practical compression, and the counting proof that no lossless compressor can shrink every input.

article.title: Data Compression
article.source: Algorithms, 4th Edition — Robert Sedgewick and Kevin Wayne, Princeton University

exercise.prompt: Build a Huffman tree for a short sentence, assign each symbol a prefix-free code, and compare the encoded bit length with fixed-width encoding.

COMP.12.note: CMU’s systems course explains locality, cache blocks, the hierarchy from registers to storage, and why access patterns often dominate real program performance.

article.title: Lecture 11: Memory Hierarchy
article.source: Carnegie Mellon University — 15-213 Introduction to Computer Systems

exercise.prompt: Benchmark summing a large matrix row-by-row and column-by-column. Compare the timings and explain the result using spatial locality and cache lines.

COMP.13.note: Goldberg’s classic tutorial explains representation, rounding error, guard digits, gradual underflow, IEEE 754, and the system-level consequences of finite precision.

article.title: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic
article.source: David Goldberg — Oracle reprint of ACM Computing Surveys

exercise.prompt: In your main programming language, test 0.1 + 0.2, repeated addition, equality near zero, NaN, positive infinity, and negative zero. Explain each result.

LING.01.note: The Annual Review separates deliberately constructed languages from naturally changing languages, while showing that both exhibit systematic phonology, grammar, vocabulary and social use.

exercise.prompt: Create a tiny language with a sound inventory, word-order rule, plural rule and ten-word vocabulary, then describe how ordinary use could make those rules drift over generations.

LING.02.note: Leiden University's course demonstrates the comparative method through regular sound correspondences, reconstruction and the Indo-European family rather than treating Proto-Indo-European as a recorded language.

exercise.prompt: Compare a small set of cognates across three Indo-European languages, mark regular sound correspondences and propose one reconstructed ancestral form.

LING.03.note: The Ask-a-Linguist overview distinguishes linguistic determinism from weaker linguistic-relativity claims and reflects the field's rejection of the strong popular version.

article.title: The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis
article.source: The LINGUIST List — Ask a Linguist

exercise.prompt: Take one claimed language-thought effect and separate vocabulary availability, attention, memory, categorisation, cultural practice and the stronger claim that thought is impossible without a word.

LING.04.note: The Unicode Standard surveys alphabetic, abjad, syllabic, abugida and logographic systems through the practical problem of representing their characters digitally.

exercise.prompt: Classify twelve scripts as alphabet, abjad, abugida, syllabary, logography or mixed system, and state what linguistic unit each basic sign represents.

LING.05.note: Stanford's entry presents the evidence and arguments around innate language capacity while distinguishing broad biological preparedness from specific Universal Grammar proposals.

exercise.prompt: Build the strongest poverty-of-the-stimulus argument you can, then list alternative explanations based on statistical learning, cognition, interaction and cultural evolution.

LING.06.note: The Annual Review explains current debates about pidgin and creole formation, contact ecologies and the problems with treating all creoles as one exceptional language type.

article.title: Pidgins and Creoles: Debates and Issues

exercise.prompt: Compare a pidgin and a creole by social history, native-speaker status, vocabulary sources, grammar and community identity without assuming a universal one-generation pathway.

LING.07.note: UNESCO frames language revitalisation as community-led work involving education, intergenerational transmission, documentation, technology, public services and language rights.

exercise.prompt: Design a ten-year revitalisation plan covering fluent elders, children, teacher training, orthography, media, public domains, digital tools and community ownership.

LING.08.note: The British Museum explains the decree's three scripts and how comparison, earlier work and Champollion's insight made Egyptian hieroglyphs readable again.

article.title: Everything You Ever Wanted to Know About the Rosetta Stone

exercise.prompt: Explain why a trilingual inscription helps decipherment, then distinguish identifying proper names from proving the phonetic and grammatical values of an entire script.

LING.09.note: The open linguistics textbook classifies widening, narrowing, amelioration, pejoration, metaphor and metonymy as recurring pathways of semantic change.

exercise.prompt: Research five words whose meanings changed and classify each change as widening, narrowing, amelioration, pejoration, metaphor, metonymy or another documented pathway.

LING.10.note: The International Phonetic Association's official chart maps consonants, vowels, suprasegmentals and diacritics to articulatory categories and standard symbols.

exercise.prompt: Transcribe ten words from your own accent, labelling each consonant by place, manner and voicing and each vowel by height, backness and rounding.

LING.11.note: The paper begins from the linguistic fact that signed languages are natural human languages with their own phonology, morphology, syntax and communities, not encoded spoken language.

article.title: Including Signed Languages in Natural Language Processing
article.source: Julie A. Hochgesang et al. — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Compare one signed and one spoken language across phonological units, word formation, syntax, discourse, regional variation and the role of physical modality.

LING.12.note: Stanford's treatment of translating Chinese philosophy shows how lexical range, grammar, historical concepts and philosophical commitments make translation an interpretive argument rather than word substitution.

exercise.prompt: Compare three translations of one short passage, identify where wording encodes interpretation, and write an annotated translation explaining each unavoidable trade-off.

THEO.01.note: Yale's Thessalonians course models how Pauline letters are read as occasional correspondence and directly addresses chronology, community setting, and disputed authorship.

exercise.prompt: Choose one Pauline letter and outline its sender, recipients, occasion, major argument, and current scholarly authorship status.

THEO.02.note: The Stanford entry provides the broader philosophical history of hermeneutics and the disciplined interpretation of texts, meaning, context, and understanding.

exercise.prompt: Interpret one short biblical passage in three stages: historical-literary context, textual claim, and contemporary application, keeping the stages distinct.

THEO.03.note: Yale's course treats canon formation historically, including the gradual recognition of texts and differences between communities rather than a single one-time decision.

exercise.prompt: Build a timeline of major Hebrew Bible and New Testament canon milestones, noting where different Christian traditions retain different collections.

THEO.04.note: Bible.org's scholarly overview lays out the literary relationships among Matthew, Mark, and Luke and compares the main proposed source theories.

exercise.prompt: Place one triple-tradition passage from Matthew, Mark, and Luke side by side and mark identical wording, omissions, additions, and changed order.

THEO.05.note: CSNTM explains why manuscripts matter and provides a concrete entry into the surviving witnesses that textual critics compare.

article.title: Why Manuscripts?
article.source: Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts

exercise.prompt: Compare two textual variants using manuscript age, geographical spread, transcriptional difficulty, and internal context; then defend a preferred reading.

THEO.06.note: The Israel Antiquities Authority introduces the discovery, date range, languages, contents, and significance of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

article.title: Introduction to the Dead Sea Scrolls
article.source: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library — Israel Antiquities Authority

exercise.prompt: Sort examples of scrolls into biblical manuscripts, apocryphal works, and sectarian writings, then explain what each category can and cannot establish.

THEO.07.note: The Israel Antiquities Authority's historical background places the scrolls within Hellenistic and Roman Judea and the diverse Jewish groups of the Second Temple period.

article.title: Historical Background
article.source: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library — Israel Antiquities Authority

exercise.prompt: Create a comparison chart for Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, revolutionary movements, and the early Jesus movement, including sources and uncertainties.

THEO.08.note: This historian-written overview uses Nicaea and Chalcedon to show how imperial politics, episcopal authority, and precise Christological language interacted in the councils.

exercise.prompt: Make a council table for Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon listing date, controversy, principal decision, and later dissent.

THEO.09.note: The Stanford entry surveys major theodicies and defenses while distinguishing attempts to explain evil from attempts to show logical compatibility.

exercise.prompt: Compare free-will, soul-making, and skeptical-theist responses to one concrete case of suffering, including the strongest objection to each.

THEO.10.note: Smarthistory connects theology, institutional conflict, vernacular scripture, visual culture, and print in a broad introduction to the Protestant Reformation.

exercise.prompt: Trace one Reformation dispute from the original church practice through Luther's objection, print circulation, political adoption, and Catholic response.

THEO.11.note: This joint Greek Orthodox Archdiocese and Hellenic Bible Society project introduces the Septuagint as the ancient Greek translation used widely in early Christianity.

article.title: About Septuagint.Bible
article.source: Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America and Hellenic Bible Society

exercise.prompt: Compare one Old Testament quotation in the New Testament with its Septuagint and Masoretic Hebrew-based English forms, then describe the meaningful differences.

THEO.12.note: Stanford's philosophy-of-religion overview situates cosmological, teleological, ontological, moral, and evidential arguments alongside major objections.

exercise.prompt: Steelman one classical argument for God as numbered premises and a conclusion, then write the strongest objection and a possible reply.

ART.01.note: Smarthistory reconstructs Brunelleschi's demonstration and Alberti's later codification, showing linear perspective as a geometric viewing system rather than a general measure of realism.

exercise.prompt: Construct a one-point-perspective room with horizon line, station point, vanishing point, orthogonals and repeated floor tiles that diminish consistently.

ART.02.note: The Met connects nineteenth-century colour science to Neo-Impressionist experiments in simultaneous contrast, optical mixture, divisionism and pointillism.

exercise.prompt: Place identical grey swatches on different coloured grounds, record the apparent changes, and build a small image using optical rather than palette mixing.

ART.03.note: The National Gallery defines chiaroscuro through modelling with light and dark, while Smarthistory separates the more extreme theatrical darkness of tenebrism.

exercise.prompt: Light one object from a single side and make two studies: one using gradual chiaroscuro modelling and another using a tenebrist jump from darkness to illumination.

ART.04.note: The Met's technical study of Thomas Cole shows how microscopy, X-radiography, infrared imaging and pigment analysis reveal both ancient and newly industrialised colours in one artist's practice.

article.title: Modern Pigments Found in Thomas Cole's Paintings Shed New Light on the Artist's Practice

exercise.prompt: Build a pigment timeline for natural ultramarine, Prussian blue, synthetic ultramarine, chrome yellow and modern organic pigments, including cost, chemistry and conservation risks.

ART.05.note: The Met traces how Japanese prints altered European cropping, flattened space, colour, everyday subject matter and asymmetrical composition rather than merely supplying exotic motifs.

exercise.prompt: Compare one ukiyo-e print with one European Japoniste work and mark borrowed choices in cropping, viewpoint, contour, pattern, depth and subject matter.

ART.06.note: MoMA presents the Bauhaus as an experimental school joining fine art, craft, industry, architecture and social ideas across its Weimar, Dessau and Berlin phases.

exercise.prompt: Redesign one household object using a Bauhaus-style brief that balances function, manufacture, materials, geometry, affordability and visual clarity.

ART.07.note: MoMA's New Typography exhibition places hierarchy, asymmetry, sans-serif type, photography and information design within the Central European avant-garde and Bauhaus context.

exercise.prompt: Typeset the same short announcement three ways, changing family, weight, size, measure, leading, kerning and hierarchy while keeping the words identical.

ART.08.note: Getty's formal-analysis guide treats composition through line, shape, value, balance, emphasis, movement and the active relationship between positive and negative space.

exercise.prompt: Reduce one image to black positive shapes and white negative shapes, then move one element at a time and record changes in balance, tension, direction and emphasis.

ART.09.note: The House of European History places Van Meegeren within a wider history of counterfeiting, provenance, expert judgement and scientific authentication rather than celebrating him as a folk hero.

exercise.prompt: Design an authentication plan using provenance, stylistic comparison, support dating, imaging, pigment and binder analysis, and explain why no single test proves authorship.

ART.10.note: The National Gallery explains preventive care, examination, scientific analysis, cleaning and restoration as documented, approved interventions constrained by material evidence and reversibility concerns.

exercise.prompt: Write a treatment proposal distinguishing original material, ageing, dirt, varnish, old restoration and loss, then justify what should be preserved, removed, stabilised or visually reintegrated.

ART.11.note: The National Gallery of Art connects Impressionism's outdoor practice to portable tube paints and rail travel while also emphasizing modern life, light, brushwork and exhibition culture.

article.title: What Is Impressionism? 4 Things to Know

exercise.prompt: Paint or photograph the same outdoor scene at three times of day and identify how portability, speed, changing light and modern pigments alter the working method.

ART.12.note: MoMA's account of Duchamp's readymades shows that modern art did not simply abandon realism after photography; artists challenged medium, authorship, skill, beauty and the institutional definition of art.

exercise.prompt: Choose an ordinary object and argue for or against its presentation as art using selection, context, intention, craft, originality, audience and institutional framing.

MUSC.01.note: The tuning overview explains why fixed-pitch instruments need temperament, how equal divisions make every key usable, and what interval purity is sacrificed.

exercise.prompt: Calculate a pure 3:2 fifth and a twelve-tone-equal-tempered fifth from the same starting frequency, then measure the discrepancy in cents across a circle of fifths.

MUSC.02.note: UNSW's music-acoustics material connects periodic vibration, fundamentals, integer-multiple partials, resonance and instrument timbre using audible examples.

exercise.prompt: Synthesize one fundamental plus its first eight harmonics, change their amplitudes, and describe how the perceived timbre changes while pitch stays constant.

MUSC.03.note: The cross-cultural study finds both shared and culture-specific emotional cues, showing that the Western major-happy/minor-sad association is real for many listeners but not a universal acoustic law.

article.title: Harmonic Organisation Conveys Both Universal and Culture-Specific Cues for Emotional Expression in Music

exercise.prompt: Create matched major and minor versions of one melody, vary tempo and timbre independently, and ask listeners which feature most changes perceived emotion.

MUSC.04.note: Open Music Theory develops species counterpoint as simultaneous independent melodies and then connects those constraints to imitation and fugal writing.

exercise.prompt: Write eight bars of first-species two-voice counterpoint, checking melodic independence, consonance, contrary motion, voice crossing and treatment of perfect intervals.

MUSC.05.note: The digital-audio course explains timbre, spectra, masking and reconstruction, providing the foundation for missing fundamentals and other psychoacoustic effects.

article.title: Digital Audio
article.source: University of California, Irvine — Christopher Dobrian

exercise.prompt: Remove the fundamental from a harmonic complex, compare perceived pitch with a spectrogram, then create a repeating Shepard-tone sequence and explain the octave ambiguity.

MUSC.06.note: UCI's Max cookbook gives a concrete account of attack, decay, sustain and release as a control signal used to shape amplitude and other synthesis parameters.

article.title: ADSR Amplitude Envelope
article.source: University of California, Irvine — Max Cookbook

exercise.prompt: Build one oscillator into a filter and ADSR envelope, then make plucked, bowed, brass-like and pad-like presets by changing only waveform, cutoff and envelope timing.

MUSC.07.note: The Library of Congress recording-registry essay documents Gregory Coleman's six-second break and its extraordinary afterlife across sampling, hip-hop, jungle and electronic music.

article.title: Amen, Brother — The Winstons
article.source: Library of Congress National Recording Registry

exercise.prompt: Slice one drum break into hits, rearrange it at three tempos, and document how chopping, pitch, time-stretching and layering turn the same recording into different rhythmic vocabularies.

MUSC.08.note: Roland's history explains the 808's analog voice circuits, sequencer, commercial failure, discontinuation and later adoption across hip-hop, techno and pop.

exercise.prompt: Program a sixteen-step pattern using kick, snare, clap and hi-hat, then alter decay, tuning, accents and swing to hear why the machine behaves like an instrument rather than a static sample bank.

MUSC.09.note: Antares' official history connects Andy Hildebrand's geophysical signal-processing work to real-time pitch detection, correction and the deliberately audible zero-retune-speed effect.

article.title: About AutoTune: Voice Technology and History

exercise.prompt: Process the same vocal with slow, medium and zero retune speed, then compare pitch accuracy, transitions, vibrato, naturalness and the stylised hard-tuned effect.

MUSC.10.note: The University of Iowa demonstration frames hall design through reverberation, absorption, reflections, clarity and the trade-off between warmth and intelligibility.

article.title: Concert Hall Acoustics
article.source: University of Iowa Department of Physics and Astronomy

exercise.prompt: Estimate reverberation time for two rooms using volume and absorption, then predict effects on intimacy, clarity, bass warmth, speech and orchestral blend.

MUSC.11.note: Open Music Theory treats meter as interacting pulse layers, providing the foundation for hearing and notating cross-rhythm and polyrhythmic structures.

exercise.prompt: Clap a 3:2 and then a 4:3 polyrhythm, place both rhythms on a shared subdivision grid, and identify the points where attacks coincide.

MUSC.12.note: EBU R 128 explains the industry shift from peak normalization toward measured programme loudness, true-peak limits and loudness range, which reduces the reward for mastering everything louder.

article.title: Loudness Normalisation and Permitted Maximum Level of Audio Signals

exercise.prompt: Create two masters with different compression and limiting but loudness-normalize them to the same LUFS value, then compare punch, fatigue, transients and loudness range.

SCRN.01.note: UC Press's description of Kuleshov's own writings identifies juxtaposition as the source of meanings not contained in either shot alone.

article.title: Kuleshov on Film
article.source: Lev Kuleshov — University of California Press

exercise.prompt: Edit the same neutral face against food, a coffin and a child at play, then ask viewers what emotion or intention they inferred from each sequence.

SCRN.02.note: The critical article examines Campbell's model as an influential storytelling tool while challenging its dominance, cultural selectivity and claim to universality.

article.title: One Myth to Rule Them All and in the Darkness Bind Them: A Critical Examination of Joseph Campbell's The Hero's Journey

exercise.prompt: Map one film onto the Hero's Journey, mark stages that must be stretched or omitted, then outline a different story whose structure resists the template.

SCRN.03.note: BFI's discussion of filmmakers who break classical grammar makes the normal continuity system visible: screen direction, eyelines, matching action and the 180-degree axis.

article.title: 4 Hard-and-Fast Rules of Filmmaking… and How The Passion of Joan of Arc Breaks Them

exercise.prompt: Shoot a short two-person exchange twice: once with consistent axis, eyelines and match-on-action, and once with deliberate violations; compare spatial comprehension.

SCRN.04.note: The ASC manual's scope shows cinematography as an integration of lenses, exposure, lighting, colour science, sensors, composition and production workflow.

exercise.prompt: Shoot one scene with two focal lengths and two lighting ratios while preserving exposure, then compare perspective, depth, facial rendering, contrast and emotional emphasis.

SCRN.05.note: The Academy's sound-and-music guide explains production sound, dialogue replacement, sound effects and Foley through practical classroom activities.

article.title: Sound and Music Activities Guide
article.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

exercise.prompt: Mute a one-minute scene and rebuild footsteps, cloth, props, ambience and designed effects from recorded household objects, synchronising each sound to picture.

SCRN.06.note: Blackmagic's official training separates technical correction from creative grading and teaches scopes, shot matching, primary balance, secondary isolation and look development.

exercise.prompt: Balance three mismatched shots with scopes before creating a look, then make warm-cool and low-high contrast variants while preserving skin and neutral references.

SCRN.07.note: The Academy's Jurassic Park programme documents the landmark blend of animatronics, stop-motion knowledge, practical photography and CGI rather than framing effects as a simple either-or choice.

article.title: Jurassic Park
article.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

exercise.prompt: Break one creature shot into practical, digital and compositing layers and explain how shared lighting, camera motion, contact, shadows, texture and scale sell the integration.

SCRN.08.note: McCloud's own presentation introduces comics as a visual language where sequence, simplification, panel choice and reader inference create time and action between images.

exercise.prompt: Tell the same action in three six-panel pages using different panel transitions and gutter sizes, then compare how much motion and time the reader must infer.

SCRN.09.note: The Open University's film-music resource treats music as structurally related to image, character, mood and narrative, providing a foundation for analysing recurring themes and leitmotifs.

article.title: Using Film Music in the Classroom

exercise.prompt: Compose a short leitmotif for one character and transform its tempo, harmony, orchestration and contour for safety, threat, loss and return.

SCRN.10.note: The storytelling principle is treated as setup and payoff rather than a literal requirement that every object must become plot machinery.

article.title: Chekhov’s Gun — Everything You Need to Know

exercise.prompt: Audit a short story scene by scene, marking setup, reminder, escalation and payoff; remove details that neither deepen character, atmosphere nor causality.

SCRN.11.note: The Library of Congress traces the Production Code from industry self-regulation through stricter enforcement and eventual replacement by ratings, making its creative pressure historically concrete.

article.title: When ‘Pre-’ Met ‘Code’ — Eighty Years Ago Today

exercise.prompt: Take one prohibited subject and write two versions of a scene: explicit and Code-era implied, using framing, dialogue, reaction, ellipsis, metaphor and off-screen space.

SCRN.12.note: BFI's cinematography tour explains how Academy, widescreen and Scope formats arose from technical and commercial systems and then became compositional choices.

exercise.prompt: Frame the same scene in 1.33:1, 1.85:1 and 2.39:1 without cropping afterward, then compare faces, groups, environment, movement and negative space.

MAKE.01.note: The ACS review explains the Maillard reaction as a network beginning with reducing sugars and amino groups and producing aromas, colours and texture changes that depend strongly on heat, water activity and pH.

article.title: Control of Maillard Reactions in Foods: Strategies and Chemical Mechanisms
article.source: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry — ACS

exercise.prompt: Brown identical onion or bread samples under different moisture, temperature and pH conditions, then compare colour, aroma, texture and time to browning.

MAKE.02.note: University of Minnesota Extension distinguishes lactic-acid, yeast and other food fermentations while emphasizing salt, acidity, oxygen control, temperature and safe handling.

exercise.prompt: Plan a vegetable fermentation with ingredient mass, salt percentage, temperature, oxygen exclusion, pH checks, spoilage signs and a discard rule.

MAKE.03.note: The ACS material explains chocolate manufacture through cocoa-butter crystallisation, heating, cooling and controlled formation of the stable crystal structure responsible for gloss and snap.

article.title: The Chemistry of Romance, Flavor, and Drink: Roses, Chocolate, and Wine

exercise.prompt: Temper one batch correctly and let another cool without seeding or temperature control, then compare gloss, snap, contraction, texture and fat bloom over several days.

MAKE.04.note: The Specialty Coffee Association connects brew ratio, total dissolved solids and extraction yield, correcting the oversimple rule that sour always means under-extracted and bitter always means over-extracted.

exercise.prompt: Brew the same coffee at three grind sizes while holding dose and water constant, record brew time and taste, and separate strength from extraction balance.

MAKE.05.note: The research explains how gliadin-rich and glutenin-rich protein mixtures produce different viscous, elastic and strain-hardening behaviour underlying dough extensibility and strength.

article.title: Flow of Gluten with Tunable Protein Composition: From Stress Undershoot to Stress Overshoot and Strain Hardening

exercise.prompt: Mix and wash a small dough to isolate gluten, then compare development after short mixing, intensive mixing and resting using stretch, windowpane and gas-retention tests.

MAKE.06.note: Penn State's guide reduces cheesemaking to its controlling decisions: milk treatment, starter culture, acidification, rennet coagulation, curd cutting, cooking, draining, salting and ageing.

exercise.prompt: Create a decision tree showing how acid versus rennet coagulation, curd size, cooking, pressing, salt, moisture, rind organisms and ageing produce different cheese families.

MAKE.07.note: The Scotch Whisky Association traces malting, mashing, fermentation, distillation and oak maturation and distinguishes legal requirements from marketing mythology.

exercise.prompt: Trace starch to bottled whisky and mark where enzymes, yeast, still shape, cut points, oak extraction, oxidation, evaporation and blending alter the final spirit.

MAKE.08.note: The Met distinguishes pattern welding—forge-welded bars arranged and twisted for structure and pattern—from crucible or watered steels often grouped loosely under the Damascus label.

article.title: Techniques of Decoration on Arms and Armor

exercise.prompt: Diagram a pattern-welded billet through stacking, forge welding, drawing, twisting, cutting and restacking, then contrast it with historical crucible steel.

MAKE.09.note: The American Ceramic Society connects glassblowing craft to viscosity, temperature control, thermal expansion, annealing and the non-crystalline structure of glass.

article.title: Scientific Glassblowing—Part Science, Part Art, All Awesome

exercise.prompt: Plot a qualitative glass-working temperature curve and mark gathering, blowing, shaping, strain point, annealing and the risks of uneven cooling.

MAKE.10.note: The American Ceramic Society introduces ceramics as inorganic non-metallic materials and provides the materials-science foundation for clay transformation, sintering and glassy glaze layers.

exercise.prompt: Create a kiln schedule and materials map for one glazed clay body, identifying water loss, burnout, quartz change, sintering, vitrification, glaze melting and cooling defects.

MAKE.11.note: Japan's only museum devoted to carpentry tools presents timber selection, marking, hand tools, post-and-beam framing, joinery and the repairable traditions of temple and tea-house construction.

exercise.prompt: Model a mortise-and-tenon or scarf joint from card or soft wood and identify the surfaces resisting tension, compression, shear, rotation and withdrawal.

MAKE.12.note: The Met explains natural-dye practice through fibres, mordants and the unusual reduction-oxidation chemistry that makes insoluble indigo enter cloth and turn blue in air.

article.title: The Materials and Techniques of American Quilts and Coverlets

exercise.prompt: Draw the indigo vat cycle from insoluble pigment through chemical reduction, dissolved leuco-indigo, fibre uptake, air oxidation and repeated dipping for depth.

SPRT.01.note: StatsBomb explains expected goals as a probabilistic model trained on historical shots and makes clear that values vary because models use different features and data quality.

article.title: What is xG? How is it calculated?

exercise.prompt: Build a simple shot table with distance, angle, body part, assist type and outcome, then estimate which variables should raise or lower scoring probability and why.

SPRT.02.note: SABR's research guide defines sabermetrics as the search for objective knowledge about baseball and shows how questions, data quality and context matter beyond the Moneyball story.

exercise.prompt: Choose one traditional baseball statistic and design a context-adjusted alternative, stating the decision it should improve and the biases it still cannot remove.

SPRT.03.note: British Cycling's retrospective documents Brailsford's one-percent framing while placing it among coaching, talent, technology, sport science and organizational changes rather than attributing success to tiny tweaks alone.

article.title: Sir Dave Brailsford at British Cycling — A Career Retrospective

exercise.prompt: Break one performance goal into ten contributing systems, estimate the likely effect and measurement cost of improving each, and reject changes whose claimed gains cannot be tested.

SPRT.04.note: The consensus statement defines internal and external training load, explains why monitoring is useful, and emphasizes individual context instead of universal workload thresholds.

article.title: Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement
article.source: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance — PubMed

exercise.prompt: Plan a four-week training block with objective external load, subjective internal load, recovery markers, progression, deloading and rules for changing the plan when responses differ.

SPRT.05.note: Joyner and Coyle frame elite endurance through the interaction of maximal oxygen uptake, lactate threshold and movement economy rather than treating any one number as destiny.

article.title: Endurance Exercise Performance: The Physiology of Champions
article.source: M. J. Joyner and E. F. Coyle — PubMed

exercise.prompt: Compare two hypothetical runners with different VO2 max, fractional threshold and running economy, then explain why the athlete with the larger VO2 max need not be faster.

SPRT.06.note: The official Court judgment records how transfer fees after contract expiry and nationality quotas conflicted with EU freedom-of-movement law for workers.

article.title: Judgment of the Court of 15 December 1995 — Bosman, Case C-415/93
article.source: Court of Justice of the European Union — EUR-Lex

exercise.prompt: Trace the pre-Bosman and post-Bosman career path of an out-of-contract EU player, separating employment mobility, transfer compensation, squad quotas and later market consequences.

SPRT.07.note: FIFA's Training Centre analyses contemporary principles such as blocks, third-player combinations and counter-pressing while showing tactics as coordinated behaviours, not just formation diagrams.

exercise.prompt: Analyse one match in possession, transition and out of possession, recording shape, pressing triggers, rest defence, overloads, rotations and adaptations to the opponent.

SPRT.08.note: The paper exposes the probabilistic assumptions beneath Elo, including expected scores, update sensitivity and the special difficulty of modelling draws and team sports.

article.title: Understanding and Pushing the Limits of the Elo Rating Algorithm
article.source: Leszek Szczecinski and Aymen Djebbi — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Implement Elo updates for four players, vary the K-factor and expected-score scale, and show how upset results, inactivity, draws and new entrants affect ratings.

SPRT.09.note: The German ghost-game study uses COVID-era empty stadiums as a natural experiment and finds that crowd effects vary by league rather than explaining all of home advantage.

article.title: Does Crowd Support Drive the Home Advantage in Professional Football? Evidence from German Ghost Games during the COVID-19 Pandemic
article.source: Kai Fischer and Justus Haucap — Journal of Sports Economics

exercise.prompt: Design a home-advantage model with travel, familiarity, crowd, referee decisions, team strength and schedule, then explain why before-after empty-stadium comparisons can still be confounded.

SPRT.10.note: The university module introduces linear and angular kinematics, kinetics, force plates and motion analysis as tools for explaining movement rather than merely judging how technique looks.

article.title: Introduction to Sport and Exercise Biomechanics

exercise.prompt: Record a jump or throw in slow motion, estimate joint angles and centre-of-mass motion, and draw the external forces and moments that produce the movement.

SPRT.11.note: WADA's current operating guidelines explain longitudinal biological monitoring, adaptive limits, expert review, sample requirements and how the passport complements direct substance detection.

exercise.prompt: Create a fictional longitudinal blood profile, add plausible altitude, illness and doping scenarios, and describe why expert review and chain-of-custody evidence are needed before sanction.

SPRT.12.note: The systematic review found widespread high risk of bias, weak reporting, overfitting and little external validation, so current models should not be treated as dependable individual injury forecasts.

article.title: Just How Confident Can We Be in Predicting Sports Injuries? A Systematic Review of Existing Musculoskeletal Injury Prediction Models in Sport
article.source: Garrett S. Bullock et al. — Sports Medicine / PubMed

exercise.prompt: Audit an injury model for leakage, class imbalance, calibration, missing data, overfitting, external validation and decision usefulness, then distinguish prediction from preventable cause.

HIST.01.note: Australian Geographic places the 1932 military cull within soldier-settlement farming, drought, crop damage and later wildlife-management policy, correcting the meme that Australia formally declared a conventional war.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite the Emu War as a policy case study with stakeholders, ecological causes, military objectives, measured outcomes, media framing and the later fence-and-bounty alternatives.

HIST.02.note: Smithsonian's account follows pepper and other Asian spices through Venice, Portuguese ocean routes and Dutch monopoly power while rejecting the myth that spices mainly disguised rotten meat.

exercise.prompt: Trace one spice from growing region to European table across producers, regional traders, ports, empires, monopolies and consumers, marking where value and coercive power accumulated.

HIST.03.note: The Library of Congress guide separates documented Gutenberg history from legend and explicitly notes that printing began in East Asia centuries before European movable-metal-type printing.

article.title: The Gutenberg Bible at the Library of Congress: Introduction

exercise.prompt: Compare manuscript copying, woodblock printing and movable type by setup cost, marginal copy cost, error correction, labour, speed, scale, censorship and access.

HIST.04.note: The debunk focuses on the hypothesis's calendar mistake and the independent chronologies supplied by tree rings, radiocarbon dating, astronomical observations and non-European records.

article.title: Phantom Time Hypothesis — the Supposedly ‘Missing’ Fortnight in 1752

exercise.prompt: Build an independent-evidence matrix for the disputed centuries using European documents, Islamic and Chinese chronology, eclipses, comets, dendrochronology, radiocarbon and archaeology.

HIST.05.note: Eric Cline's overview rejects a single-cause invasion story and presents the collapse as a connected-system failure involving warfare, migration, political unrest, disrupted trade, earthquakes and climate stress.

article.title: Interview: The Mysterious Bronze Age Collapse with Eric Cline
article.source: World History Encyclopedia — Eric H. Cline

exercise.prompt: Draw the Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean as a network of palaces, trade, food, metals and security, then model how several smaller shocks could cascade through it.

HIST.06.note: The National Archaeological Museum's dedicated project presents the fragments, inscriptions, imaging research and reconstructed astronomical functions without calling the device a modern digital computer.

article.title: The Mysteries of the Mechanism of Antikythera

exercise.prompt: Choose one dial and reconstruct the required input, gear ratio, output cycle and astronomical purpose, distinguishing evidence on fragments from modern reconstruction.

HIST.07.note: The Open University compares the sparse ancient and much later accounts and shows why Caesar, the Serapeum and the Arab-conquest story cannot be merged into one cinematic destruction event.

article.title: The Library of Alexandria — The Destruction of the Library

exercise.prompt: Create a source timeline for Caesar's fire, later Roman decline, the Serapeum destruction and the Arab-conquest legend, recording source dates and what each actually claims.

HIST.08.note: The museum history integrates fission science, dispersed industrial sites, military organization, secrecy, uranium and plutonium production, bomb design and the continuing ethical and environmental legacy.

article.title: The Manhattan Project
article.source: National Museum of Nuclear Science & History / Atomic Heritage Foundation

exercise.prompt: Map Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Hanford, Chicago and military command by scientific task, industrial bottleneck, workforce, secrecy requirement, hazard and ethical decision.

HIST.09.note: The historical article reconstructs how contemporaries interpreted the Strasbourg outbreak through disease, divine punishment and social conditions; mass psychogenic illness is a serious proposal, not a proved diagnosis.

article.title: Divine Punishment or Disease? Medieval and Early Modern Approaches to the 1518 Strasbourg Dancing Plague
article.source: Lynneth J. Miller — Dance and History bibliography

exercise.prompt: Compare ergot poisoning, deliberate ritual, neurological disease and mass psychogenic illness by expected symptoms, spread, contemporary evidence and weaknesses.

HIST.10.note: The Nuclear Museum traces radium-dial production, corporate denial, bone damage, litigation and the workers' influence on radiation protection and occupational safety.

article.title: The Radium Girls
article.source: National Museum of Nuclear Science & History / Atomic Heritage Foundation

exercise.prompt: Build a failure chain from brush practice through internal exposure, delayed symptoms, company knowledge, medical evidence, legal barriers, compensation and later safety standards.

HIST.11.note: Boston's official centenary account uses city-archive photographs and emphasizes the untested tank, victims, litigation and resulting movement toward professional engineering oversight.

article.title: 100 Years Ago Today: Molasses Crashes Through Boston’s North End
