exercise.prompt: Perform a modern hazard review of the tank covering design pressure, material, foundation, temperature, filling rate, inspection, warning signs, emergency planning and regulatory approval.

HIST.12.note: The Open Encyclopedia of Anthropology explains that 'cargo cult' bundled diverse Melanesian religious and political movements into a colonial academic category, often obscuring local critiques of unequal exchange and power.

article.title: Cargo Cults
article.source: Open Encyclopedia of Anthropology — Lamont Lindstrom

exercise.prompt: Take one named Melanesian movement and describe its colonial setting, theology, leadership, political demands and local meaning before judging whether the label cargo cult clarifies or distorts it.

RSCH.01.note: The Open Science Collaboration's large replication project is the landmark empirical starting point, while its interpretation should be read with attention to effect sizes and methodological debate.

article.title: Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science

exercise.prompt: Choose three different definitions of replication success and explain how the same replication project can yield different headline percentages.

RSCH.02.note: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn demonstrate how undisclosed analytic flexibility can manufacture statistically significant results without fabricating data.

article.title: False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant
article.source: Joseph P. Simmons, Leif D. Nelson, and Uri Simonsohn — Psychological Science

exercise.prompt: List ten researcher degrees of freedom in a hypothetical study and mark which decisions should be preregistered before seeing the data.

RSCH.03.note: Sense about Science opens the peer-review black box, explaining editorial screening, reviewer roles, limitations, alternatives, and post-publication review.

article.title: Peer Review: The Nuts and Bolts

exercise.prompt: Write a mock peer review with separate sections for summary, major concerns, minor concerns, reproducibility, and recommendation.

RSCH.04.note: Keshav's author-hosted page links the original three-pass reading method and updated supporting resources.

exercise.prompt: Apply the first two passes to one paper and produce the five-C summary: category, context, correctness, contributions, and clarity.

RSCH.05.note: The updated CONSORT explanation provides the scientific rationale behind transparent randomized-trial design and reporting, including randomization, allocation, blinding, outcomes, and analysis.

article.title: CONSORT 2025 Explanation and Elaboration: Updated Guideline for Reporting Randomised Trials

exercise.prompt: Take a published randomized trial and audit its abstract, randomization, allocation concealment, attrition, outcomes, and analysis against CONSORT items.

RSCH.06.note: Hernán and Robins provide a free, rigorous book that frames causal questions through counterfactuals, exchangeability, DAGs, confounding, selection, and longitudinal treatment.

article.title: Causal Inference: What If
article.source: Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins

exercise.prompt: Draw a DAG containing an exposure, outcome, confounder, mediator, and collider, then justify which variables should and should not be adjusted for.

RSCH.07.note: Cochrane's handbook chapter gives precise definitions and empirical evidence for publication, time-lag, selective-reporting, citation, language, and location biases.

article.title: Considering Bias and Conflicts of Interest Among the Included Studies
article.source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions

exercise.prompt: Create a funnel-plot thought experiment showing how selectively missing small null studies can shift a pooled estimate.

RSCH.08.note: Cochrane's meta-analysis chapter explains effect measures, weighting, heterogeneity, fixed and random effects, and why inappropriate pooling can mislead.

article.title: Analysing Data and Undertaking Meta-Analyses
article.source: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions

exercise.prompt: Combine three fictional study estimates using inverse-variance weights, then explain how heterogeneity changes the interpretation of the pooled result.

RSCH.09.note: OSF's current guide defines preregistration and gives concrete practices for specifying hypotheses, exclusions, variables, models, outcomes, and contingencies in advance.

exercise.prompt: Draft a short preregistration for a simple experiment, including hypothesis, sample, exclusions, variables, primary outcome, analysis, and deviation policy.

RSCH.10.note: Button and colleagues explain how low power reduces true-effect detection, inflates observed effect sizes among significant findings, and weakens reproducibility.

article.title: Power Failure: Why Small Sample Size Undermines the Reliability of Neuroscience
article.source: Katherine S. Button et al. — Nature Reviews Neuroscience / PubMed

exercise.prompt: Calculate power across several sample sizes for one expected effect, then compare false-negative risk and the precision of the estimated effect.

RSCH.11.note: Mangel and Samaniego's historical analysis is the scholarly source behind the aircraft-survivability example and explains the selection problem in data from returning aircraft.

article.title: Abraham Wald’s Work on Aircraft Survivability
article.source: Marc Mangel and Francisco J. Samaniego — Journal of the American Statistical Association

exercise.prompt: Invent a dataset containing only successful cases, identify what observations are missing by design, and show how analyzing survivors alone reverses the decision.

RSCH.12.note: Cuellar's modern treatment explains the prosecutor's fallacy through likelihood ratios and the separation between probability of evidence given a hypothesis and probability of the hypothesis given evidence.

article.title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy and Expert Testimony: A Modern Take Using Likelihood Ratios

exercise.prompt: Build a base-rate example in which evidence is rare among innocent people but innocence remains plausible, then compute both conditional probabilities explicitly.

ECON.01.note: Open Yale Courses develops game theory through players, strategies, payoffs, information, timing, dominance, equilibrium, repeated interaction and applications rather than presenting it as a collection of puzzles.

exercise.prompt: Model one strategic situation by listing players, available actions, payoffs, information, order of moves and whether commitments are credible.

ECON.02.note: Yale's opening lecture derives the Prisoner's Dilemma from its payoff structure and uses it to distinguish individually dominant choices from collectively better outcomes.

deeper.title: Lecture 21 — Repeated Games: Cooperation versus the End Game

exercise.prompt: Write a Prisoner's Dilemma payoff matrix, identify dominant strategies and equilibrium, then change repetition, patience and punishment to make cooperation sustainable.

ECON.03.note: Yale's lecture introduces best responses and Nash equilibrium while emphasizing that equilibrium means no profitable unilateral deviation, not fairness, efficiency or happiness.

article.title: Lecture 5 — Nash Equilibrium: Bad Fashion and Bank Runs

exercise.prompt: Find every pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in three small payoff matrices and identify which equilibria are Pareto-efficient, risky or coordination-dependent.

ECON.04.note: The Nobel overview explains Schelling's work on tacit coordination, focal points, credible commitments, conflict and segregation without reducing it to a party-game trick.

article.title: Conflict and Cooperation through the Lens of Game Theory

exercise.prompt: Give several people the same no-communication meeting problem, compare their chosen focal points, and explain which shared conventions made one answer salient.

ECON.05.note: The Nobel overview contrasts simple privatization-or-state-control prescriptions with Ostrom's evidence that communities can build durable institutions for shared resources under identifiable conditions.

article.title: Economic Governance: The Organization of Cooperation

exercise.prompt: Design governance rules for one shared resource covering boundaries, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, local participation and adaptation over time.

ECON.06.note: Yale's lecture treats moral hazard as hidden action after a contract and separates it from adverse selection, incentives, monitoring and risk sharing.

exercise.prompt: Design an insurance or employment contract that balances risk protection with incentives, then identify behaviours the principal cannot directly observe.

ECON.07.note: The IMF explanation derives gains from trade through opportunity cost and specialization, including the counterintuitive case where one country is absolutely more productive in every activity.

exercise.prompt: Give two producers different productivities in two goods, calculate opportunity costs, choose specialization and show a trade price that benefits both.

ECON.08.note: The 2020 Nobel overview connects auction formats, private and common values, the winner's curse, bidding strategies and the design of real spectrum auctions.

article.title: The Quest for the Perfect Auction

exercise.prompt: Run first-price and second-price sealed-bid auctions with private values, compare truthful and shaded bidding, then add uncertain common value to create a winner's-curse risk.

ECON.09.note: The Bank of England explains that commercial-bank lending creates matching deposits, while repayment destroys bank money and central-bank reserves play a different settlement role.

article.title: Money Creation in the Modern Economy

exercise.prompt: Write simplified bank and borrower balance sheets before a loan, immediately after lending, after spending and after principal repayment, tracking deposits, loans and reserves.

ECON.10.note: The Stanford study examines technology adoption when a product becomes more valuable as compatible users grow, separating installed-base effects from product quality and marketing.

article.title: Adoption of Technologies with Network Effects: An Empirical Examination of the Adoption of Automated Teller Machines
article.source: Garth Saloner and Andrea Shepard — Stanford Graduate School of Business

exercise.prompt: Model adoption of a platform whose value rises with users, then test how interoperability, multi-homing, switching cost, subsidies and congestion alter winner-take-most dynamics.

ECON.11.note: The Nobel overview presents Spence's signalling model, where education or another observable action can convey hidden productivity only when its costs differ across types.

exercise.prompt: Construct a separating signal by assigning different signal costs to high- and low-quality types, then show when pooling or imitation destroys credibility.

ECON.12.note: The Nobel explanation presents mechanism design as reverse game theory: define desired outcomes, information constraints and incentives, then design rules that make truthful or socially useful behaviour rational.

exercise.prompt: Design rules for allocating one scarce resource when participants privately know their values, then test incentive compatibility, efficiency, budget balance and participation.
